elements.id-string-6: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has recently emerged as a groundbreaking model in the field of image segmentation.
elements.id-string-7: Nevertheless, both the original SAM and its medical adaptations necessitate slice-by-slice annotations, which directly increase the annotation workload with the size of the dataset.
elements.id-string-8: We propose MedLSAM to address this issue, ensuring a constant annotation workload irrespective of dataset size and thereby simplifying the annotation process.
elements.id-string-9: Our model introduces a few-shot localization framework capable of localizing any target anatomical part within the body.
elements.id-string-10: To achieve this, we develop a Localize Anything Model for 3D Medical Images (MedLAM), utilizing two self-supervision tasks: relative distance regression (RDR) and multi-scale similarity (MSS) across a comprehensive dataset of 14,012 CT scans.
elements.id-string-11: We then establish a methodology for accurate segmentation by integrating MedLAM with SAM.
elements.id-string-12: By annotating only six extreme points across three directions on a few templates, our model can autonomously identify the target anatomical region on all data scheduled for annotation.
elements.id-string-13: This allows our framework to generate a 2D bounding box for every slice of the image, which are then leveraged by SAM to carry out segmentations.
elements.id-string-14: We conducted experiments on two 3D datasets covering 38 organs and found that MedLSAM matches the performance of SAM and its medical adaptations while requiring only minimal extreme point annotations for the entire dataset.
elements.id-string-15: Furthermore, MedLAM has the potential to be seamlessly integrated with future 3D SAM models, paving the way for enhanced performance.

elements.id-string-20: \begin{figure}[t!] \vspace{-0.6cm}  \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{seg_pipe.pdf} \caption{The overall segmentation pipeline of MedLSAM operates as follows. Given a dataset of any size, MedLSAM first applies a localization process (MedLAM) to identify the six extreme points (in the z, x, and y directions) of any anatomical region of interest. This process results in the generation of a 3D bounding box encompassing the targeted organ or structure. Subsequently, for each slice within this 3D bounding box, a corresponding 2D bounding box is generated. These 2D bounding boxes are then utilized by the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to carry out precise segmentation of the target anatomy, thereby automating the entire segmentation process.}  \end{figure}
elements.id-string-21: \par The Segment Anything Model (SAM) \cite{kirillov2023segment} has recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in a broad range of segmentation tasks due to its ability to manage diverse objects.
elements.id-string-22: Previous research has explored the application of SAM to medical image segmentation \cite{cheng2023sam, he2023sam, MSA, MedSAM, huang2023segment, he2023accuracy, zhang2023customized, mazurowski2023segment, zhang2023segment}.
elements.id-string-23: Particularly with fine-tuned medical adaptations \cite{MSA, MedSAM}, SAM models have achieved impressive performance in this specialized area.
elements.id-string-24: However, SAM's application to medical image segmentation poses a significant challenge due to its requirement for manual annotations.
elements.id-string-25: These include labeled points or bounding boxes that delineate the segmentation region, which are both time-intensive and costly to produce.
elements.id-string-26: In this paper, we introduce MedLSAM, an automated medical image segmentation model designed to significantly reduce the annotation workload.
elements.id-string-27: As illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig:MedLSAM}, MedLSAM employs a two-stage methodology.
elements.id-string-28: The first stage involves a few-shot localization framework that automatically identifies the positions of target organs within volumetric medical images.
elements.id-string-29: The subsequent stage utilizes the bounding boxes generated in the first stage by applying the SAM model to execute precise image segmentation.
elements.id-string-30: The result is a fully autonomous pipeline that eliminates the need for manual intervention.
elements.id-string-31: The few-shot localization framework, MedLAM, is an extension of our previous work \cite{lei2021contrastive} and is premised on the observation that the spatial distribution of organs maintains strong similarities across different individuals.
elements.id-string-32: Our previous studies trained the model on a relatively smaller dataset.
elements.id-string-33: In contrast, this current study significantly expands the dataset to include 14,012 CT scans from 16 different datasets.
elements.id-string-34: This allows us to train a unified, comprehensive model capable of localizing structures across the entire body.
elements.id-string-35: The training process involves a projection network that predicts the 3D physical offsets between any two patches within the same image, thereby mapping every part of the scans onto a shared 3D latent coordinate system.
elements.id-string-36: While our localization approach is robust, we acknowledge that individual variations in anatomical positioning could result in different anatomical structures sharing the same latent coordinates across various images.
elements.id-string-37: To mitigate this issue, we refine our localization accuracy by extracting pixel-level features from our points of interest.
elements.id-string-38: This method enables us to identify the most similar feature within the vicinity of the initially localized point, thus enhancing the overall localization accuracy.
elements.id-string-39: Our approach is inspired by the self-supervised learning tasks proposed in \cite{yao2021one, yan2022sam}, which strive to maximize the similarity between the original and augmented instances of the same image point and minimize the similarity between different points.
elements.id-string-40: This technique improves the accuracy and precision of our model's localization.
elements.id-string-41: For the segmentation stage, we employ the original SAM and the well-established MedSAM \cite{MedSAM} as the foundation for our segmentation process.
elements.id-string-42: MedSAM, previously fine-tuned on a comprehensive collection of medical image datasets, has exhibited considerable performance in 2D and 3D medical image segmentation tasks.
elements.id-string-43: The use of such a robust model bolsters the reliability and effectiveness of our proposed pipeline.
elements.id-string-44: The effectiveness of MedLSAM is validated through experiments on two 3D datasets comprising 38 organs.
elements.id-string-45: The results demonstrate that MedLSAM parallels the performance of SAM and its medical adaptations while significantly reducing the burden of manual annotation.
elements.id-string-47: In this section, we elucidate the mechanisms underpinning MedLAM's functionality.
elements.id-string-48: Initially, in Section \ref{sec:2.2}, we explore the training of MedLAM, during which global anatomical coordinates and local image features are extracted from any given point within a scan, aiding in identifying the most similar point within a query scan.
elements.id-string-49: Subsequently, in Section \ref{sec:2.3}, we detail the inference process of MedLAM and its integration with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to give rise to the comprehensive MedLSAM model.
elements.id-string-51: Our MedLAM model, as illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig:training}, comprises two main components: Relative Distance Regression (RDR) and Multi Scale Similarity (MSS).

elements.id-string-54: We then extract two large image patches from $\bm{v}$, which serve as the source for further extractions.
elements.id-string-55: These large patches undergo a variety of transformations to produce two pairs of patches, namely, the original patch pair $(\bm{x_q}, \bm{x_s})$ and the transformed patch pair $(\bm{x_q'}, \bm{x_s'})$.

elements.id-string-68: \par More specifically, as shown in Fig. \ref{fig:mss}, the inputs to our MSS process include multi-scale feature maps extracted from $\bm{x_s}$ and $\bm{x'_s}$, along with a chosen point $c_1$ from $\bm{x_s}$, whose corresponding point in $\bm{x'_s}$ is the $c'_1$.
elements.id-string-69: We extract the feature vectors corresponding to point $c_1$ from the various scale feature maps of $\bm{x_s}$, and we compute the similarity between these feature vectors and the corresponding scale feature maps in $\bm{x'_s}$.
elements.id-string-70: After resizing the resulting similarity maps to the original image size, we aggregate them.
elements.id-string-71: This process allows us to pinpoint the location within $\bm{x'_s}$ that exhibits the highest similarity to point $c_1$, thereby further refining our localization.

elements.id-string-78: \par Our MedLAM model is trained on an extensive set of 16 datasets, which collectively comprise a total of 14,012 CT scans.
elements.id-string-79: These scans encompass various regions of the human body, providing comprehensive anatomical coverage.
elements.id-string-80: An overview of the training datasets is provided in Table~\ref{tab:dataset}.
elements.id-string-81: The diverse and abundant training data ensures the robustness and generalizability of our model across different medical imaging contexts.
elements.id-string-82: \par To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we integrate MedLAM with two segmentation backbones: SAM\cite{kirillov2023segment} and MedSAM\cite{MedSAM}.
elements.id-string-83: We test these combined models on two CT segmentation datasets: 1) StructSeg19 Task1 dataset \footnote{https://structseg2019.grand-challenge.org/Home/} for the 22 head-and-neck (HaN) organs with 50 scans; 2) the WORD dataset \cite{luo2022word} for the 16 abdomen organs with 120 scans.
elements.id-string-84: For both datasets, we randomly select five scans as support volumes.
elements.id-string-85: For each organ in these scans, we compute the extreme coordinates and average the coordinates and features across the five images.
elements.id-string-86: This process generates an average representation of latent coordinates and features for each extreme point of the organ, which are then utilized in the succeeding stages of MedLAM as depicted in Sec.

elements.id-string-115: After validating the localization performance of MedLAM, we proceeded to examine the segmentation performance of the proposed MedLSAM framework.
elements.id-string-116: In our experiments, the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) was employed as a measure to gauge the accuracy of our method.
elements.id-string-117: MedLSAM utilizes the localization information from MedLAM, together with either SAM or MedSAM, to perform segmentation tasks.
elements.id-string-118: In addition to the automatic localizations generated by MedLAM, we also included manual bounding boxes in our evaluation.
elements.id-string-119: These were simulated based on the ground-truth masks, following the same approach used for generating bounding boxes in MedSAM.
elements.id-string-120: During training, a bounding box prompt was generated from each ground-truth mask, with a random perturbation of 0-20 pixels introduced to mimic the potential inaccuracies that would be present in manually-drawn bounding boxes.
elements.id-string-121: The DSC scores of StructSeg Task1 dataset are shown in Table \ref{tab:structseg}, it is clear that MedLAM performed comparably to manual localisation in the context of small organs.
elements.id-string-122: For example, organs like the left and right eyes, MedLAM based SAM and MedSAM have DSC values of around 61-67\%, which are close to the DSC values of 67-69\% from manual localization.
elements.id-string-123: For minute organs such as the left and right lenses, MedLAM shows a similar DSC value to manual localisation (around 22\% for SAM and 16\% for MedSAM).
elements.id-string-124: However, MedLAM based SAM and MedSAM have lower performance in the context of the mandible (left and right), with DSC values of 48.3\% and 43.5\% for SAM and only 9.0\% and 2.6\% for MedSAM, compared to manual localization DSC values of 85.3\% and 80.4\%.

elements.id-string-126: Meanwhile, our evaluation on the WORD dataset for abdominal organ segmentation, as shown in Table \ref{tab:word}, revealed that MedLAM demonstrated robust performance for organs such as the left and right kidneys.
elements.id-string-127: For instance, when integrated with SAM, the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) reached 78.5\% for the left kidney, and escalated to an impressive 83.0\% for the right kidney.
elements.id-string-128: When combined with MedSAM, the model maintained satisfactory performance with a DSC of 66.2\% for the left kidney and 62.3\% for the right kidney.
elements.id-string-129: However, for smaller organs like the adrenal gland, both SAM and MedSAM yielded lower DSC values under 4\% in comparison to a manual localization DSC of 18.7\%.
elements.id-string-131: The presented work introduced MedLSAM, the first completely automated medical adaptation of the SAM model, designed to significantly alleviate the annotation workload in the segmentation of medical images.
elements.id-string-132: By cleverly integrating MedLAM, a few-shot localization framework, with SAM, the system was able to achieve comparable performance to SAM and its medical adaptations, yet required only minimal extreme point annotations for the entire dataset.
elements.id-string-133: This endeavor was fueled by the observation that the spatial distributions of organs across different patients maintain strong similarities.
elements.id-string-134: Consequently, MedLAM was designed to project every part of the scans onto a shared 3D latent coordinate system, accurately localizing target anatomical parts within the body.
elements.id-string-135: Coupling this approach with SAM's segmentation capabilities led to an efficient and accurate process for image segmentation.
elements.id-string-136: Moreover, MedLSAM demonstrated its effectiveness across two 3D datasets covering 38 different organs, providing robust evidence of its versatility.
elements.id-string-137: Importantly, this automated approach is not burdened by an increased annotation workload as data size increases.
elements.id-string-138: It also holds promise for direct integration with potential future 3D SAM models in the medical field, which could further enhance its performance and utility.

elements.id-string-147: Our model introduces a 3D localization foundation model capable of localizing any target anatomical part within the body.
elements.id-string-148: To achieve this, we develop a Localize Anything Model for 3D Medical Images (MedLAM), utilizing two self-supervision tasks: unified anatomical mapping (UAM) and multi-scale similarity (MSS) across a comprehensive dataset of 14,012 CT scans.
elements.id-string-149: By annotating several extreme points across three directions on a few templates, our model can autonomously identify the target anatomical region on all data scheduled for annotation.
elements.id-string-150: This allows our framework to generate a 2D bbox for every slice of the image, which is then leveraged by SAM to carry out segmentation.
elements.id-string-151: We carried out comprehensive experiments on two 3D datasets encompassing 38 distinct organs.
elements.id-string-152: Our findings are twofold: 1) MedLAM is capable of directly localizing any anatomical structure using just a few template scans, yet its performance surpasses that of fully supervised models; 2) MedLSAM not only aligns closely with the performance of SAM and its specialized medical adaptations with manual prompts but achieves this with minimal reliance on extreme point annotations across the entire dataset.

elements.id-string-161: \par Recently, there has been an increasing interest in the field of computer vision to develop large-scale \textit{foundational models} that can concurrently address multiple visual tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation.
elements.id-string-162: For instance, CLIP \citep{radford2021learning}, aligning a vast number of images and text pairs collected from the web, could recognize new visual categories using text \textit{prompts}.
elements.id-string-163: Similarly, GLIP \citep{li2022grounded, zhang2022glipv2}, which integrates object detection with phrase grounding in pre-training using web-sourced image-text pairs, boasts strong zero-shot and few-shot transferability in object-level detection tasks.
elements.id-string-164: On the segmentation front, the \textit{Segment Anything Model (SAM)} \citep{kirillov2023segment} has recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in a broad range of segmentation tasks with appropriate prompts, e.g. points, bounding box (bbox) and text.
elements.id-string-165: \par As foundational models increasingly demonstrate their prowess in general computer vision tasks, the medical imaging domain, characterized by limited image availability and high annotation costs, is taking keen notice of their potential.
elements.id-string-166: Such challenges in medical imaging underscore the pressing need for foundational models, drawing greater attention from researchers \citep{zhang2023challenges}.
elements.id-string-167: Some studies have endeavored to design self-supervised learning tasks tailored to dataset characteristics, pre-training on a vast amount of unlabeled data, and then fine-tuning on specific downstream tasks to achieve commendable results \citep{wang2023mis, zhou2023foundation, vorontsov2023virchow}.
elements.id-string-168: In contrast, other works have focused on pre-training with large annotated datasets, either to fine-tune on new tasks \citep{huang2023stu} or to enable direct segmentation without the necessity of further training or fine-tuning \citep{butoi2023universeg}.
elements.id-string-169: Overall, these models offer myriad advantages: they simplify the development process, reduce dependence on voluminously labeled datasets, and bolster patient data privacy.
elements.id-string-170: \par In the field of segmentation, models such as SAM and its medical adaptations \citep{MSA, MedSAM, cheng2023sam, he2023sam, huang2023segment, he2023accuracy, zhang2023customized, mazurowski2023segment, zhang2023segment} have demonstrated significant potential.
elements.id-string-171: Both \cite{huang2023segment} and \cite{cheng2023sam} have collected extensive medical image datasets and conducted comprehensive testing on SAM.
elements.id-string-172: They discovered that, while SAM exhibits remarkable performance on certain objects and modalities, it is less effective or even fails in other scenarios.
elements.id-string-173: This inconsistency arises from SAM's primary training on natural images.
elements.id-string-174: To enhance SAM's generalization in medical imaging, studies like \cite{MSA, MedSAM} have fine-tuned the original SAM using a large annotated medical image dataset, thereby validating its improved performance over the base SAM model in test datasets.
elements.id-string-175: Despite these advancements, the models still require manual prompts, such as labeled points or bounding boxes, which remains a substantial limitation due to the associated time and financial implications.
elements.id-string-176: \par In scenarios requiring manual annotation prompts, annotating 3D images proves especially time-consuming and labor-intensive.
elements.id-string-177: A single 3D scan often contains dozens or even hundreds of slices.
elements.id-string-178: When each slice comprises multiple target structures, the annotation requirements for the entire 3D scan grow exponentially\citep{wang2018deepigeos, lei2019deepigeos}.
elements.id-string-179: To eliminate this vast annotation demand and facilitate the use of SAM and its medical variants on 3D data, an effective approach would be to automatically generate suitable prompts for the data awaiting annotation.
elements.id-string-180: While this could be achieved by training a detector specifically for the categories to be annotated, it introduces the additional burden of annotating data for detector training, and the detectable categories remain fixed\citep{baumgartner2021nndetection}.
elements.id-string-181: A more optimal solution would be to develop a universal localization model for 3D medical images.
elements.id-string-182: This model would only require users to provide minimal annotations to specify the category of interest, allowing for direct localization of the desired target in any dataset without further training.
elements.id-string-183: \par However, to the best of our knowledge, foundational models specifically tailored for 3D medical image localization are still limited.
elements.id-string-184: In the domain of 2D medical image localization, MIU-VL \citep{qin2022medical} stands out as a pioneering effort.
elements.id-string-185: This approach ingeniously marries pre-trained vision-language models with medical text prompts to facilitate object detection in medical imaging.
elements.id-string-186: However, the application of these pre-trained models to specialized medical imaging domains, particularly 3D modalities like CT scans, remains challenging.
elements.id-string-187: This limitation is attributable to a significant domain gap, as these models were originally trained on 2D natural images.
elements.id-string-188: \par \textbf{In response to the lack of localization foundation models for 3D medical images and the persistent need for extensive interaction in SAM, we introduce MedLSAM in this paper}.
elements.id-string-189: MedLSAM is an automated medical image segmentation solution that combines the Localize Anything Model for 3D Medical Image (MedLAM), a dedicated 3D localization foundation module designed for localizing any anatomical structure using a few prompts, with existing segmentation foundation models.
elements.id-string-190: The first stage involves MedLAM to automatically identify the positions of target structures within volumetric medical images.
elements.id-string-191: In the subsequent stage, the SAM model uses the bboxes from the first stage to achieve precise image segmentation.

elements.id-string-208: \par Over recent years, large-scale pre-trained deep learning vision models have marked remarkable milestones with models like ResNet\citep{he2016deep}, ConvNeXt\citep{liu2022convnet}, Vision Transformers (ViT)\citep{dosovitskiy2020image}, and DINO\citep{caron2021emerging}.

elements.id-string-210: \par In the realm of medical image analysis, the challenges are compounded by concerns of data privacy and the often tedious nature of annotation tasks, making the procurement of large-scale annotated data both challenging and costly.
elements.id-string-211: This elevates the significance of visual foundational models in the field.

elements.id-string-215: \par Turning the attention to segmentation, a key aspect within medical imaging, there has been a surge of interest in the application of SAM for medical image segmentation \citep{cheng2023sam, he2023sam, MSA, MedSAM, huang2023segment, he2023accuracy, zhang2023customized, mazurowski2023segment, zhang2023segment}.

elements.id-string-219: Intriguingly, comprehensive studies by \cite{huang2023segment} and \cite{cheng2023sam} have delved into the optimal prompts for SAM's application in medical imaging.

elements.id-string-300: \par  As shown in Fig. \ref{fig:subpatch}(a), for a target anatomical structure, we can generate a single minimal 3D bounding box (bbox) $\bm{B}$ that completely encompasses the organ by locating its six extreme points in three dimensions:  $[\bm{z}_{min}, \bm{z}_{max}, \bm{x}_{min}, \bm{x}_{max}, \bm{y}_{min}, \bm{y}_{max}]$.

elements.id-string-402: In this study, we have introduced MedLSAM, the first completely automated, two-stage medical adaptation of the SAM model, designed to significantly alleviate the annotation workload in the segmentation of medical images.
elements.id-string-403: The first stage, MedLAM, serves as a pioneering localization foundation model, capable of precisely identifying anatomical structures in 3D medical images.

elements.id-string-405: Together, these components form a fully automated pipeline that significantly reduces the reliance on manual annotations and annotated data.
elements.id-string-408: \textcolor{black}{Recent advancements in foundation models have shown significant potential in medical image analysis.
elements.id-string-409: However, there is still a gap in models specifically designed for medical image localization.
elements.id-string-410: To address this, we introduce MedLAM, a 3D medical foundation localization model that accurately identifies any anatomical part within the body using only a few template scans.
elements.id-string-411: MedLAM employs two self-supervision tasks: unified anatomical mapping (UAM) and multi-scale similarity (MSS) across a comprehensive dataset of 14,012 CT scans.
elements.id-string-412: Furthermore, we developed MedLSAM by integrating MedLAM with the Segment Anything Model (SAM).
elements.id-string-413: This innovative framework requires extreme point annotations across three directions on several templates to enable MedLAM to locate the target anatomical structure in the image, with SAM performing the segmentation.
elements.id-string-414: It significantly reduces the amount of manual annotation required by SAM in 3D medical imaging scenarios.
elements.id-string-415: We conducted extensive experiments on two 3D datasets covering 38 distinct organs.
elements.id-string-416: Our findings are twofold: 1) MedLAM can directly localize anatomical structures using just a few template scans, achieving performance comparable to fully supervised models; 2) MedLSAM closely matches the performance of SAM and its specialized medical adaptations with manual prompts, while minimizing the need for extensive point annotations across the entire dataset.
elements.id-string-417: Moreover, MedLAM has the potential to be seamlessly integrated with future 3D SAM models, paving the way for enhanced segmentation performance.} Our code is public at \href{https://github.com/openmedlab/MedLSAM}{https://github.com/openmedlab/MedLSAM}.

elements.id-string-419: \par Recently, there has been an increasing interest in the field of computer vision to develop large-scale \textit{foundation models} that can concurrently address multiple visual tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation.
elements.id-string-420: \par As foundation models increasingly demonstrate their prowess in general computer vision tasks, the medical imaging domain, characterized by limited image availability and high annotation costs, is taking keen notice of their potential.
elements.id-string-421: Such challenges in medical imaging underscore the pressing need for foundation models, drawing greater attention from researchers \citep{zhang2023challenges}.
elements.id-string-422: \par \textcolor{black}{As a crucial component of medical image analysis, medical image localization encompasses tasks such as keypoint detection\citep{chen2021fast, wan2023multi}, organ localization\citep{xu2019efficient,navarro2020deep, hussain2021cascaded, navarro2022unified}, and disease detection\citep{yan2018deeplesion, zhang2018automatic}.
elements.id-string-423: However, to the best of our knowledge, foundation models specifically designed for medical image localization tasks remain very limited.
elements.id-string-424: This limitation is attributable to a significant domain gap, as these models were originally trained on 2D natural images.}
elements.id-string-425: \par \textcolor{black}{At the same time, in the field of medical image segmentation,  models such as SAM and its medical adaptations \citep{MSA, cheng2023sam, he2023sam, huang2023segment, he2023accuracy, zhang2023customized, mazurowski2023segment, zhang2023segment} have demonstrated significant potential, even achieving performance comparable to fully supervised segmentation models in certain tasks \citep{MedSAM}.} Despite these advancements, these models still require manual prompts, such as labeled points or bounding boxes.
elements.id-string-426: However, a single 3D scan often contains dozens or even hundreds of slices.
elements.id-string-427: When each slice comprises multiple target structures, the annotation \textcolor{black}{demands} for the entire 3D scan grow exponentially \citep{wang2018deepigeos, lei2019deepigeos}.
elements.id-string-428: While this could be achieved by training a detector specifically for the categories to be annotated, it introduces the additional burden of annotating data for detector training, and the detectable categories remain fixed \citep{baumgartner2021nndetection}.
elements.id-string-429: A more optimal solution would be to develop a foundation localization model for 3D medical images that only requires minimal user input to specify the category of interest, allowing for direct localization of the desired target in any dataset without further training.
elements.id-string-430: \textcolor{black}{This challenge underscores the urgent need for a 3D medical localization foundation model.}
elements.id-string-431: \par \textcolor{black}{To address the lack of foundation models for 3D medical image localization, we introduce the \textbf{Localize Anything Model for 3D Medical Images (MedLAM)}.
elements.id-string-432: MedLAM is a specialized 3D localization foundation model designed to accurately locate any anatomical structure using minimal prompts.
elements.id-string-433: Additionally, we integrated MedLAM with the SAM model to create \textbf{MedLSAM}, a framework that significantly reduces the need for extensive manual interaction in SAM while demonstrating the potential to achieve competitive performance.
elements.id-string-435: The result is a fully autonomous pipeline that \textcolor{black}{minimizes} the need for manual intervention.

elements.id-string-512: We have conducted a comparative analysis between MedLAM and \textcolor{black}{four well-established methodologies: 1) DetCo~\cite{xie2021detco}, an unsupervised contrastive learning framework for object detection; 2) Mask R-CNN~\cite{he2017mask}, a general fully-supervised detection method; 3) nnDetection~\cite{baumgartner2021nndetection}, which serves as a highly robust fully-supervised medical image detection baseline; 4) MIU-VL~\cite{qin2023medical}, a pioneer work utilizing visual-language foundation model for zero-shot medical image localization.}
elements.id-string-513: \textcolor{black}{For the implementation of DetCo, we apply the identical preprocessing protocol utilized for MedLAM, training it on the same dataset of 14,012 CT scans with a pretrained 3D ResNet50 backbone\cite{feichtenhofer2019slowfast}.
elements.id-string-514: During inference, we employ the Multi-Scale Similarity (MSS) process described in Section \ref{sec:4.2}, where we average the features of each landmark across the support volume to accurately localize the most similar point within the query volume.
elements.id-string-515: To ensure a fair comparison, we maintained the same support/query split as MedLAM for each experiment.}
elements.id-string-516: For Mask R-CNN, we utilize the 3D implementation in MedicalDetectionToolkit\cite{jaeger2020retina} \footnote{https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/medicaldetectiontoolkit}.
elements.id-string-517: \textcolor{black}{For the organ extreme point detection task, each extreme point of an organ was treated as a separate class in both Mask R-CNN and nnDetection models.
elements.id-string-518: To ensure a thorough and comprehensive performance evaluation, we implemented a five-fold cross-validation approach for both models.}
elements.id-string-519: \par Regarding MIU-VL, we follow the procedures outlined in the original paper, using GLIP \citep{li2022grounded} as the foundation model for zero-shot detection.
elements.id-string-520: To generate the required text prompts for MIU-VL, we utilized ChatGPT \citep{ouyang2022training} to generate prompts containing descriptions of [COLOR], [SHAPE], [LOCATION], and [CLASS] for different organs.

elements.id-string-526: On the WORD dataset, MedLAM's average IoU of 56.6\% surpasses nnDetection by 11.2\%, but is slightly lower than Mask R-CNN.

elements.id-string-528: \textcolor{black}{For the self-supervised DetCo method, we have observed that it is only capable of localization within a coarse range.

elements.id-string-609: \textcolor{black}{In this study, we introduced MedLAM, a foundational localization model for medical images capable of identifying any anatomical structure within 3D medical images.
elements.id-string-610: By integrating it with the SAM model, we developed MedLSAM, an automated segmentation framework designed to reduce the annotation workload in medical image segmentation.}
elements.id-string-611: \textcolor{black}{We validated MedLAM and MedLSAM across two 3D datasets, covering 38 different organs.
elements.id-string-612: The results demonstrate that MedLAM, using only a few support samples, can achieve performance comparable to or better than existing fully supervised models.
elements.id-string-613: MedLAM’s ability to localize anatomical structures efficiently and accurately underscores its potential for broader applications in medical imaging, including rapid and automatic localization of user-specified landmarks or regions of interest.
elements.id-string-614: This makes it particularly suited for scenarios requiring flexible and scalable localization without the need for extensive fine-tuning.}
elements.id-string-615: \par \textcolor{black}{While MedLSAM shows promise in reducing annotation workloads, it still does not match the performance of fully supervised models such as nnU-Net, especially in cases involving organs with significant anatomical abnormalities.
elements.id-string-616: This highlights the need for further refinement of prompt-based segmentation methods.}
elements.id-string-617: \par \textcolor{black}{Future work should focus on enhancing MedLAM’s versatility and integrating it with emerging generalist medical AI (GMAI)\cite{moor2023foundation} applications.
elements.id-string-618: Doing so could further improve its generalizability and close the performance gap with fully supervised models, while also reducing the resources and time required for medical imaging analysis.
